shots.text: What if a giant asteroid
was about to hit Earth?
Not a small one.
A rock ten kilometres wide,
the same size as the one that wiped out the dinosaurs.
In this video, we'll follow it step by step,
from the first warning
to the world it leaves behind.
And by the end, you'll see why
space agencies are already practising for this exact day.
Chapter one. Twenty four hours to impact.
Telescopes spot it
far beyond the Moon,
racing toward us at about twenty kilometres every second.
That's fast enough
to cross the entire United States in under four minutes.
With only one day left,
there's no time to launch a spacecraft and push it away.
So the only question left
is where it will land.
Cities empty overnight.
Highways jam.
People head for high ground,
and deep underground.
And then, in the final hour,
a new star appears in the sky,
and it's getting brighter.
Everyone on Earth is about to find out
what ten kilometres of rock can do.
Chapter two. Impact.
The asteroid reaches the top of the atmosphere,
a hundred kilometres up.
At twenty kilometres every second,
it punches through all of that air in about five seconds.
The air in front of it can't get out of the way.
It gets squeezed so hard
that it glows hotter than the surface of the Sun.
For anyone looking up,
the sky splits open with a blinding white light.
Let's say it comes down exactly where the dinosaur killer did,
in a shallow sea off the coast of Mexico.
This rock is so big that when its front edge touches the seabed,
its back end is still about as high as a passenger jet flies.
To an object this size, the ocean is barely a puddle.
In less than a second,
it releases about a hundred million megatons of energy.
That's billions of times the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima,
and more than ten thousand times
every nuclear weapon on Earth put together.
The asteroid doesn't just make a hole.
It vaporises.
So does the rock underneath it.
For a moment, the hole is around thirty kilometres deep,
more than three times the height of Mount Everest.
Then the walls collapse,
and the floor rebounds upward,
like a drop of water splashing back out of a pond.
Within minutes, the crater settles into a scar
about a hundred and eighty kilometres wide.
A column of molten rock and vapour blasts upward,
right out of the atmosphere.
Some of it reaches space.
The ground shakes with an earthquake
far stronger than anything ever recorded.
A blast wave races outward
with winds faster than any hurricane.
Everything within hundreds of kilometres
is flattened, burned, or buried.
Further away, the ground jumps first.
The sound of the impact arrives much later,
as a roar louder than any thunder.
That's the first few minutes.
But the crater isn't the real danger.
What comes back down is.
Chapter three. The sky catches fire.
Remember the debris that was blasted into space?
Gravity pulls it back.
Billions of tonnes of it.
Over the next few hours,
it rains down all over the planet
as tiny glassy beads and burning rock.
Every grain is a little shooting star.
Even on the far side of the planet,
people look up and see the sky fill with meteors,
as if every star is falling at once.
Trillions of them heat the upper atmosphere at the same time.
Some scientists think the whole sky glowed
like the inside of an oven,
hot enough to set fire to forests on the ground below.
And we have evidence.
Geologists have found soot and those same tiny glass beads
in a thin layer of rock all around the world,

Meanwhile, the ocean strikes back.
The impact shoves trillions of tonnes of water aside,

In twenty twenty two, scientists simulated the dinosaur impact

In the open ocean, a tsunami can travel as fast as a jet airliner.
Within two days, the waves had spread across most of the world's oceans,
some still many metres high
when they reached coastlines on the other side of the planet.
Now imagine that today.
Coastal cities around the Gulf of Mexico disappear under water within hours.
Planes are grounded.
Power grids fail.
Satellites are hit by falling debris.
For most of the world, the news arrives in fragments,
if it arrives at all.
And yet, the fire and the water are not what wiped out the dinosaurs.
The real killer is quieter.
It's the dark.
Chapter four. The long night.
The impact threw something else into the sky.
Dust, soot from the fires,
and hundreds of billions of tonnes of sulfur
from the rocks it vaporised.
High in the atmosphere, that sulfur turns into tiny droplets
that reflect sunlight back into space.
Within weeks, a veil wraps around the entire planet.
Midday starts to look like dusk.
In some places, like night.
Imagine stepping outside at noon and needing a torch to see.
The air smells of smoke.
Snow starts falling in places that have never seen it,
and it's grey with ash.
Without sunlight, plants can't make food.
Studies suggest photosynthesis almost stopped for a year or more.

shots.text: Then the cold arrives.
Some climate models suggest the planet's average temperature dropped by more than twenty degrees Celsius,
and stayed below freezing for years.
Tropical forests freeze.
Rain turns acidic.
In the oceans, the plankton die first,
then the fish that eat them,
then everything that eats the fish.
The whole food chain collapses from the bottom up.
Now think about us.
Our farms need sunlight just like the forests do.
One cold, dark year means no harvest almost anywhere on Earth.
And most countries only keep a few months of food in storage.
So the people who make it through the first day
face a much harder question.
What do eight billion people eat when the Sun disappears?
Researchers who study global catastrophes have looked at this exact problem.
Their answers sound strange, but they work.
Mushrooms grown on dead wood.
Greenhouses heated by power plants.
Even sugar made from leaves and sawdust.
Survival would depend on how fast we could switch the whole world
to food that doesn't need the Sun.
But if you could fast forward a few years,
you'd see something unexpected.
Life doesn't end.
It changes hands.
Chapter five. The world it leaves behind.
Slowly, the sky clears.
The sulfur rains out within a few years.
The dust settles. Sunlight returns.
But the climate swings the other way.
All the carbon dioxide released by the impact and the fires traps heat.
One study found that after the cold, temperatures rose by about five degrees,
and stayed high for around a hundred thousand years.
Sixty six million years ago,
when this really happened,
about three quarters of all species on Earth disappeared.
Not just the dinosaurs.
The giant sea reptiles.
The flying pterosaurs.
The ammonites,
whose shells had filled the oceans for hundreds of millions of years.
So who survived?
The small ones.
Animals that could burrow, hide,
eat seeds, or live on dead things.
Turtles.
Crocodiles.
Frogs.
Birds, the only dinosaurs that made it.
And small, furry mammals,
most of them tiny enough to hide in a hole in the ground.
With the giants gone, those mammals got their chance.
Over the next ten million years
they spread into every empty corner of the planet,
and grew into whales,
horses,
elephants,
and eventually, primates.
The plants came back too.
In rock layers just above the impact,
fossil pollen suddenly gives way to fern spores.

shots.text: Ferns were the first plants to cover the burned land.
In a strange way, we're only here
because an asteroid cleared the stage.
But this time, the giants are us.
We're big, we need a lot of food,
and our whole civilisation depends on a stable climate.
A world after impact would have no global trade,
no internet,
and no supermarkets.
What it would have is what we've saved.
Libraries.
Survivors with skills.
And places like the Global Seed Vault in Norway,
buried inside a frozen mountain,
holding more than a million samples of the world's crops.
The world it leaves behind
is colder, darker and emptier,
and then, over thousands of years, green again.
Which brings us back to the question from the very beginning.
If this could happen,
why are space agencies so calm?
Chapter six. How we stop it.
First, the good news.
Asteroids this big are incredibly rare.
A rock ten kilometres wide hits Earth
roughly once every hundred million years.
They're also the easiest to find.
NASA says it has already found more than ninety percent
of the near Earth asteroids bigger than one kilometre,
and none of them are on course to hit us for at least the next century.
The real danger is the smaller ones.
A rock a few hundred metres wide wouldn't end the world,
but it could wipe out a city, or an entire region.
And fewer than half of those have been found.
That's why the real weapon isn't a missile.
It's time.
If we spot an asteroid years or decades ahead,
we don't need to blow it up.
We just need to nudge it.
A push of just one centimetre per second, given ten years early,
adds up to thousands of kilometres by the time it reaches us.
Enough to make it miss.
There are a few ways to give that push.
Crash a spacecraft into it.
Park a heavy spacecraft beside it
and let gravity tug it off course, very slowly.
Or, for a big one with little time, set off a nuclear device nearby,
to blast vapour off one side and shove it away.
In twenty twenty two, NASA tested exactly that.
A spacecraft called DART flew eleven million kilometres
and slammed into a small asteroid moon called Dimorphos
at about six kilometres per second.
It worked.
The impact changed the moon's orbit by thirty two minutes.
For the first time ever,
humans changed the path of a natural object in space.
And Europe's Hera spacecraft is on its way there right now,
to study the crash site up close.
Meanwhile, the hunt is getting faster.
The new Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile
is scanning the whole southern sky every few nights.
And NASA is building a space telescope called NEO Surveyor,
made for one job:
finding dangerous asteroids before they find us.
The system is already being tested for real.
In early twenty twenty five,
a newly found asteroid called twenty twenty four Y R four

of hitting Earth in twenty thirty two.
Telescopes around the world tracked it,
and within weeks, the threat was ruled out.
And on the thirteenth of April, twenty twenty nine,
an asteroid called Apophis, longer than three football fields,
will pass closer to Earth than many of our satellites.
An impact has already been ruled out,
so instead of a threat, it's a free science lesson,

So, what if a giant asteroid was about to hit Earth?

there would be nothing we could do.
But that's exactly why people are watching the sky every single night.
